subject: EM
title: Natural hazards
sub: Earthquakes, volcanoes, cyclones, floods, drought, management
strategyIntro: Environmental Management has no Core or Extended split. The full exam is Paper 1 (theory: short questions, then longer questions using source material) and Paper 2 (management in context, based on one country). Most marks come from reading sources and building arguments.

strategy.title: Quote the data
points: Most marks come from graphs, tables and maps.
Use figures with units: “fell from 62% to 41%” scores; “it fell” doesn’t.
Describe the overall trend first, then give the highest, lowest or any exception.

strategy.title: The 6-mark argument
points: Usually one per paper: discuss a statement for and against.
Structure: two points for, two against, then a conclusion.
Each point needs a reason: say why it matters, not just what it is.

strategy.title: Use named examples
points: Learn one named example of an earthquake or eruption and one tropical cyclone: place, date, impacts and responses.
On Paper 2, link every answer back to the country in the source. General answers score lower.

strategy.title: Fieldwork comes up every year
points: Know sampling, quadrats, questionnaires and how to make them reliable.
Evaluate a method: one strength, one weakness, one improvement.

commandWords: Give a short fact. No explanation needed.
Say what happens or what you see. With data, quote figures and units.
Say why or how. Use “because” and link cause to effect.
Apply what you know to a new situation. Any sensible reason scores.
Give similarities or differences for both things in the same sentence.
Show working and give the unit.
Weigh up both sides and finish with a judgement.
quizIntro: These are not exam-format questions (EM has no multiple choice). Use them to check the facts are secure before you try the longer questions.
flashIntro: Say each definition out loud before you tap, then check you used the exact keywords.

flashcards.back: Crust (thin, solid), mantle (hot, semi-molten rock), outer core (liquid iron and nickel), inner core (solid).
A large slab of the Earth’s crust that moves slowly, driven by convection currents in the mantle.
Plates move towards each other; the denser oceanic plate sinks (subduction). Violent earthquakes and explosive volcanoes, e.g. Andes, Japan.
Plates move apart; magma rises to make new crust. Gentle volcanoes and small earthquakes, e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Iceland.
Plates slide past each other. Earthquakes but no volcanoes, e.g. San Andreas Fault, California.
Two continental plates push together and crumple upwards into fold mountains, e.g. the Himalayas. Earthquakes, no volcanoes.
Focus: the point underground where the earthquake starts. Epicentre: the point on the surface directly above it.
Measured on the Richter or moment magnitude scale. Each whole number up means 10 times more ground shaking.
A series of very large sea waves caused when an undersea earthquake (or eruption, landslide) suddenly moves the sea floor.
Lava flows, pyroclastic flows (fast clouds of hot gas, ash and rock), ash fall, lahars (volcanic mudflows), toxic gases.
An intense low-pressure storm with very strong winds (over 119 km/h) and heavy rain. Called hurricanes (Atlantic) and typhoons (NW Pacific).
Sea surface over about 26.5°C, warm water at least 50 m deep, 5–30° from the equator, high humidity, little wind shear.
Warm, moist air rises over the sea; water vapour condenses, releasing heat; this pulls in more air, which spins because of the Earth’s rotation.
The Earth’s rotation makes moving air curve, so storms spin. It is too weak near the equator, so cyclones do not form there.
Eye: calm, clear centre where air sinks. Eye wall: ring of the strongest winds and heaviest rain around it.
A rise in sea level caused by strong winds pushing water onshore and low pressure lifting the sea. Floods coasts; often the biggest killer.
Strong winds, storm surge, heavy rain causing floods and landslides.
They lose their supply of warm, moist air (their energy source), and friction with the land slows the winds.
Classifies hurricanes from category 1 to 5 by wind speed.
Late summer and autumn, when sea temperatures are highest.
Water covering land that is normally dry, e.g. when a river overflows its banks or the sea floods the coast.
Heavy or prolonged rain, snowmelt, saturated or impermeable ground, steep slopes, storm surges.
Urbanisation (concrete, drains), deforestation, compacted farmland, building on floodplains.
Leaves and branches catching rainfall, slowing how fast it reaches the ground.
The volume of water flowing past a point in a river each second, measured in cubic metres per second (cumecs).
Time between peak rainfall and peak discharge on a flood hydrograph. A short lag time means a higher flood risk.
The flat land beside a river that floods naturally.
A long period with much less rainfall than normal, so there is not enough water to meet demand.
Persistent high pressure (dry, sinking air), El Niño, climate change; made worse by overuse of rivers and groundwater, and deforestation.
Crop failure, livestock deaths, food shortages and famine, water rationing, wildfires, desertification, migration.
Primary: direct effects, e.g. buildings collapse. Secondary: later effects, e.g. fires, disease, homelessness, job losses.
Forecasting when and where a hazard will happen, using monitoring. Cyclones and many eruptions can be predicted; earthquakes cannot yet.
Seismometers (small earthquakes), tiltmeters (ground swelling), gas measurements, satellite heat images.
Satellites, aircraft and weather radar track the storm’s path and strength, so warnings can be issued days ahead.
Emergency plans, drills, evacuation routes, shelters, emergency supply kits and public education.
Using hazard maps to stop building in high-risk areas, e.g. floodplains or near volcanoes.
Deep foundations, steel frames, cross-bracing, rubber base isolators that absorb shaking, and light roofs.
Built structures: dams, levees (embankments), flood walls, straightened or deepened channels.
Working with nature: planting trees, restoring wetlands, floodplain zoning, flood warnings.
Short-term: food, water, shelter, medical care right after. Long-term: rebuilding homes, roads and services.

quiz.q: Tectonic plates move because of:
quiz.why: Heat from the core makes mantle rock rise, spread and sink, dragging the plates.

quiz.q: The San Andreas Fault in California is a:
quiz.why: The Pacific and North American plates slide past each other.

quiz.q: Why are there no volcanoes at conservative boundaries?
options: The crust there is too thick
Crust is neither destroyed nor created, so no magma forms
quiz.why: Magma forms where a plate melts in subduction or where plates pull apart.

quiz.q: A pyroclastic flow is:
options: A fast-moving cloud of hot gas, ash and rock
quiz.why: They can move at over 100 km/h and are the deadliest volcanic hazard.

quiz.q: Many people live near volcanoes because:
options: The land is cheap and flat
Weathered volcanic rock makes very fertile soil
quiz.why: Other reasons: geothermal energy, tourism, minerals, and people having lived there for generations.

quiz.q: Compared with a magnitude 5 earthquake, a magnitude 7 earthquake has:
quiz.why: Each step is 10 times, so two steps is 10 × 10 = 100. The energy released rises even more (about 32 times per step).

quiz.q: The main energy source of a tropical cyclone is:
options: Heat released when water vapour condenses
quiz.why: Warm seas give lots of evaporation; condensation in the clouds releases that heat, powering the storm.

quiz.q: Tropical cyclones do not form on the equator because:
options: The Coriolis effect is too weak to make them spin
quiz.why: They form between about 5° and 30° from the equator.

quiz.q: A storm surge is:
options: A rise in sea level pushed onshore by strong winds and low pressure
A tsunami caused by an earthquake
quiz.why: Low-lying coasts such as Bangladesh are most at risk.

quiz.q: Conditions in the eye of a tropical cyclone are:
options: The strongest winds and heaviest rain
Calm, with light winds and clear skies
quiz.why: Air sinks in the eye. The worst weather is in the eye wall around it.

quiz.q: In the north-west Pacific, tropical cyclones are called:
quiz.why: Hurricane (Atlantic, NE Pacific), typhoon (NW Pacific), cyclone (Indian Ocean, South Pacific).

quiz.q: Which change in a river basin would shorten the lag time?
options: Building a town with concrete surfaces and drains
quiz.why: Impermeable surfaces and drains get rainwater into the river much faster.

quiz.q: Deforestation increases flood risk because:
options: There is less interception and infiltration, so more surface runoff
quiz.why: Eroded soil also fills river channels, so they hold less water.

quiz.q: River discharge is measured in:
quiz.why: 1 cumec = 1 cubic metre per second.

quiz.q: Which is an impact of drought rather than of flooding?
quiz.why: Dry vegetation burns easily during a drought.

quiz.q: Drought is often linked to:
quiz.why: Sinking air in high pressure stops clouds forming, so there is little rain for weeks or months.

quiz.q: Which helps scientists predict a volcanic eruption?
options: Tiltmeters measuring swelling of the ground
quiz.why: Rising magma makes the volcano bulge and causes small earthquakes and gas release.

quiz.q: Rubber base isolators in buildings:
options: Absorb shaking so the building moves less
quiz.why: The building sits on flexible pads, so less of the ground movement reaches it.

quiz.q: Which is an example of soft engineering to reduce flooding?
options: Planting trees in the river basin
quiz.why: Trees increase interception and infiltration, slowing water reaching the river.

quiz.q: Which is short-term aid after a disaster?
quiz.why: Short-term aid meets immediate needs in the first days and weeks.

quiz.q: Which is a secondary impact of an earthquake?
quiz.why: Secondary impacts happen as a result of the primary ones.

examIntro: Paper 1 style. Write your answer first, then open the mark scheme. The data questions give a small table in the question: quote the figures in your answer.

exam.q: State two differences between oceanic crust and continental crust.
points: Oceanic crust is thinner
Oceanic crust is denser / heavier
Oceanic crust is younger
Oceanic crust is mainly basalt; continental mainly granite
Oceanic crust can be subducted / destroyed; continental is not

exam.q: Explain why earthquakes and volcanoes occur at destructive plate boundaries.
points: Plates move towards each other
The denser oceanic plate is subducted beneath the continental plate
Plates stick; pressure builds up and is released suddenly as an earthquake
The subducted plate melts in the mantle to form magma
Magma is less dense, so it rises through cracks and erupts as a volcano

exam.q: Two earthquakes of the same magnitude (made-up figures). Earthquake A, high-income country: magnitude 7.0, deaths 120. Earthquake B, low-income country: magnitude 7.0, deaths 45 000. (a) Calculate how many times more deaths there were in earthquake B. (b) Suggest reasons why earthquake B caused more deaths.
points: (b) Fewer earthquake-resistant buildings / weak building materials, so more collapsed
(b) Building laws not enforced
(b) Less preparation: fewer drills, emergency kits or plans
(b) Fewer emergency services, hospitals and rescue equipment
(b) Dense informal settlements / poor roads slowed rescue and aid

exam.q: State two conditions needed for a tropical cyclone to form.
points: Sea surface temperature above about 26.5°C
Warm water to a depth of at least 50 m
Between about 5° and 30° from the equator
Humid / moist air
Low wind shear

exam.q: Describe the hazards caused by a tropical cyclone when it reaches land.
points: Very strong winds damage buildings, trees and power lines
Storm surge floods low-lying coastal land
Heavy rainfall causes river flooding
Landslides on steep slopes
Flying debris injures people
Contaminated water spreads disease afterwards

exam.q: Maximum wind speed of a hurricane after it reached land (made-up figures): 0 hours – 210 km/h; 6 hours – 160 km/h; 12 hours – 120 km/h; 24 hours – 70 km/h. (a) Describe the change in wind speed. (b) Calculate the average fall in wind speed per hour over the 24 hours. (c) Explain why the hurricane weakened.
points: (a) Wind speed fell from 210 to 70 km/h
(a) Fastest fall in the first 6 hours (50 km/h)
(c) Over land there is no warm sea, so no supply of warm, moist air
(c) Less condensation, so less heat released to power the storm
(c) Friction with the land surface slows the winds

exam.q: State two physical causes of flooding.
points: Heavy or prolonged rainfall
Snowmelt
Saturated ground
Impermeable rock or frozen ground
Steep slopes
Storm surge / tropical cyclone

exam.q: Explain how urbanisation increases the risk of flooding.
points: Concrete and tarmac are impermeable, so water cannot infiltrate
More surface runoff
Drains carry water quickly to rivers, so the lag time is shorter
Fewer trees, so less interception
River discharge peaks higher and faster

exam.q: Rainfall in Town T (mm). Average year: 820; 2021: 790; 2022: 540; 2023: 410. Reservoir level at the end of each year (% full): 2021 – 85; 2022 – 52; 2023 – 30. (a) Calculate the 2023 rainfall as a percentage of the average. (b) Describe the changes shown. (c) Suggest two impacts of these changes on people in the area.
points: (b) Rainfall was below average every year and fell each year, from 790 to 410 mm
(b) Reservoir level fell from 85% to 30% full, following the fall in rainfall
(c) Water rationing / hosepipe bans
(c) Crops fail or irrigation is limited, so food prices rise
(c) Livestock die / wildfires / low rivers harm fishing and wildlife

exam.q: Give two ways buildings can be designed to withstand earthquakes.
points: Deep foundations
Steel frame / reinforced concrete
Rubber base isolators / shock absorbers
Cross-bracing
Counterweights on the roof
Light roof materials / windows that do not shatter

exam.q: Describe how people can prepare for a tropical cyclone.
points: Monitor the storm by satellite and issue warnings
Plan evacuation routes and evacuate people in time
Build cyclone shelters on stilts / raised ground
Prepare emergency kits: water, food, torch, first aid
Board up windows and tie down loose objects
Plant mangroves or build sea walls against storm surge
Run drills and public education campaigns

exam.q: “Hard engineering is the best way to reduce the risk of flooding.” Discuss this statement.
points: For: dams and levees can hold back large volumes of water, protecting towns
For: gives quick, visible protection for valuable land and buildings
For: dams can also provide HEP and water supply
Against: very expensive to build and maintain
Against: can fail or be overtopped in an extreme flood, and may move flooding downstream
Against: damages habitats; soft engineering (trees, wetlands, zoning, warnings) is cheaper and more sustainable
Conclusion: e.g. a mix works best: hard engineering for cities, soft engineering for the rest of the basin
exam.note: Two points for, two against, plus a conclusion. Max 5 without a conclusion.
